title: Fixing a dropped stitch — catching it before it unravels
subtitle: Identify where the stitch fell and work it back up with the hook
excerpt: A dropped crochet stitch shows as a loose loop dangling from the fabric. Unlike knitting, a dropped crochet stitch generally will not ladder down on its own — but it will pull the surrounding fabric out of shape if left. Working back up through the rows to retrieve it is straightforward once you know the insertion sequence.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch that has slipped off the hook or been omitted during working, leaving a loose loop in the fabric. In crochet, dropped stitches usually stay in place (unlike knitting ladders) but create a gap or reduce the stitch count.

heroPrompt: A crochet swatch with one dropped stitch visible as a dangling loop, with a crochet hook positioned to catch it, close-up showing the fix in progress.

content.text: in crochet usually means a loop that slipped off the hook before the stitch was completed, or a stitch entirely missed during a row. Crochet stitches are self-supporting — each completed stitch closes with its top loop locked — so a dropped stitch typically stays where it is rather than unravelling further. The fix depends on how many rows back the drop occurred.
Count the stitches of the current row or round. If the count is one short, a stitch was dropped or skipped somewhere.
Look across the row below for a loose loop or a wider-than-usual gap between two stitches.
If you can't see it from the current row, unravel back until you reach the dropped position.
Insert the hook into the dropped loop from front to back.
Catch the horizontal strand of yarn running directly above the dropped loop (this is the unworked yarn from the row above).
Pull this strand through the dropped loop — one dc recovered.
If there are multiple rows to recover, repeat: catch the next horizontal strand and pull through. Work up one row at a time.

items.symptom: The recovered stitch looks too large or has a visible gap
items.cause: Pulling the recovery strand too loosely
items.fix: After recovery, use the hook tip to redistribute the excess yarn into the surrounding stitches — nudge the strand sideways into the neighbouring stitches until the tension matches.

content.text: Counting stitches at the end of every row is the only reliable way to catch drops before they are buried under further rows. Using a stitch counter and placing a marker every 10 stitches makes it fast to spot a loss early.
